newsitem.title: UK: Hefty Jan debt repayment shows lively UK recovery.
newsitem.headline: Hefty Jan debt repayment shows lively UK recovery.

text.p: A massive debt repayment into the government's coffers in January underlines a lively recovery in Britain and leaves the Chancellor well on track to meet his borrowing target for the year, economists said.
Sizeable corporate tax income was a major factor in the 5.8 billion sterling repayment, suggesting Britain's firms were in better shape than had been expected in the 1995/6 tax year.
"The Chancellor of the Exchequer must be jumping for joy," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy. "This leaves him well on target for his full year forecast."
Coleman said the data may also prompt some scaling back of market expectations of borrowing forecasts for next year.
"Clearly in a pre-election phase this could not be better news for Clarke and the government," he said.
But analysts said there may well be some concerns in financial markets prompted by the strong growth, high tax revenue picture painted in Tuesday's PSBR data.

With a tight battle being fought between Chancellor Kenneth Clarke and Bank of England Governor Eddie George over whether monetary policy needs to be tightened to tame inflationary pressures, the data could ruffle Clarke's feathers.

"The PSBR figures showed bumper VAT receipts -- two billion higher than a year ago. Could that really translate into weak retail sales? I think not," said Nigel Richardson, head of bond research at Yamaichi International.

Retail sales data for January, due at 0930 GMT on Wednesday, are forecast to rise 0.3 percent on the month versus a 0.8 percent decline in December. The year-on-year rate is expected to rise to 3.9 percent from 2.9 percent previously.

Analysts said VAT revenue of 5.23 billion sterling in January, combined with 8.69 billion of income tax and 7.65 billion of corporate tax receipts, showed a fiscal situation dominated by income growth rather than spending cuts.

"The strength of tax receipts is a further sign ... of the underlying strength of activity in the economy, and ties in with suggestions that GDP growth will be revised up in 1996," said Andrew Milligan, economist at General Accident in London.
For the gilt market, the positive news that the Chancellor looks set to meet his borrowing target for this year, would be offset somewhat by the signs of a healthy economy.
But both Coleman and Peter Osler, economist at GNI, said the net effect should be supportive for gilts.
"There are signs of strength in the economy but it looks like the Chancellor will meet his target," said Osler.
"On the fundamental side, you could argue that gilts are a sell, but that's not what markets are concentrating on now."
Coleman said the 10-year gilt/Bund spread, now at 170 basis points, could slim to 160 basis points in the coming sessions.
Running up to the election, which must be held by May 22, analysts said the scope for further cuts in government spending was limited.

But despite steady expenditure in January and the risk of more cash outflows in the coming months, revenue growth would continue to show through, analysts said, keeping the government in line to meet its forecast 26.4 billion sterling borrowing requirement for the year to April 1997.
